samples.text:
The pie charts shows how students in secondary schools in one country used their time on a normal weekday and on a normal day at the weekend.

On a weekday, the biggest part of time was sleep with 35%, and school and lessons was nearly the same with 29%. Leisure and screens was 13%, meals and personal care was 9% and homework was 8%. Travel was the smallest activity at 6%. So on a weekday students used most of time for sleeping and studying.

At the weekend, students sleeped more, it was 40% of the day. The time for leisure and screens increased very much to 30%, it is more than double of the weekday. Meals and personal care went up to 12% and homework also went up to 10%. However, school and lessons fell to only 3%, and travel was 5%.

Overall, sleep took the most time in both days. On weekdays students spent a lot of time in school, but at the weekend they have much more free time for leisure and screens.
samples.why: All key figures reported accurately · brief overview placed at the end · mechanical linking and repetition · adequate vocabulary · several verb form, agreement and tense errors that do not impede communication.

samples.text:
The pie charts compare how secondary school students in one country divided their time on a typical weekday and on a typical weekend day.

Overall, sleep took up the largest share of students' time on both types of day. The main difference was that school and lessons occupied a large part of the weekday, whereas leisure and screen time dominated students' waking hours at the weekend.

On weekdays, students spent 35% of their time asleep and 29% at school or in lessons. Leisure activities and screens accounted for 13%, followed by meals and personal care at 9% and homework at 8%. Travel took up the smallest proportion, at 6%.

At weekends, the proportion of time spent sleeping rose to 40%. More noticeably, leisure and screen time more than doubled to 30%, while school and lessons dropped to only 3%. Students also spent slightly more time on meals and personal care (12%) and on homework (10%) than they did on weekdays. The share of time devoted to travel, on the other hand, remained almost the same, at 5%.
samples.why: Clear overview contrasting the two days · key differences highlighted with accurate figures · logical organisation · good range of linking devices · some less common vocabulary · frequent error-free sentences.

samples.text:
The charts illustrate how secondary school students in one country typically allocated their time across six activities on a weekday and on a weekend day.

Sleep accounted for the greatest share of time on both days, but the balance between formal education and leisure differed sharply: school dominated the waking hours of a weekday, whereas leisure and screen use largely took its place at weekends.

On a typical weekday, students slept for 35% of the day and spent almost as much time (29%) at school or in lessons. The remaining time was divided between leisure and screens (13%), meals and personal care (9%), homework (8%) and travel (6%).

At weekends, formal lessons shrank to a mere 3%, and the time released was absorbed mainly by leisure and screens, whose share rose to 30%, well over double the weekday figure. Students also slept more, with sleep accounting for 40% of the day. Interestingly, homework actually took up a slightly larger proportion of time at the weekend (10%) than during the week, and meals and personal care likewise increased, to 12%. Travel, meanwhile, was the only activity that remained virtually unchanged, at 5%.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected and contrasted · clear, well-placed overview · selective and accurate comparison of figures · cohesion handled naturally · precise vocabulary (time released was absorbed) · wide range of error-free structures.
